# Model selection as an approach {-}

## Explanation

### The basics
A simple explanation and hopefully figure of what the test does or gets at.
Model selection looks at suites of variables in otherwise comparable models.  The models are compared by some number (such as AIC, AICc, or BIC, defined later) and ranked.  The "best" (more accurately the highest-ranked) models are the best of the set, not the best in all the possible universe.  You might have not added all the needed variables to explain your data. This approach can be modified with "model averaging" that allows you to combine multiple of the highest-ranked models.

Read chapter 8 first as summary to get big picture: Burnham, Kenneth P, and David Raymond Anderson. 2008. Model Selection and Multimodel Inference: A Practical Information-Theoretic Approach. New York, NY [u.a.]: Springer.


### More technical

#### Questions and data types

- Any generalized linear model (linear regression, generalized linear models, ANOVA, ANCOVA, and more) that generates AICs can work

#### Key assumptions

- Model selection does not use p-values (models are not significant or not)
- You provide selected, well-thought-out hypotheses and compare them
- This is best suited for comparing suites of variables instead of all possible combinations
- Any higher-ranked models may not be the best model, only the best model you've tested
- To find out how of the model explains your data, you can look at weights
- You don't get to interpret the coefficients by significance like you do with regular frequentist statistics

#### Key distinctions among related methods
- This is a suggested alternative to stepwise selection [@hegyiUsingInformationTheory2011], which is strongly advised against [@mundryStepwiseModelFitting2009; @smithStepAwayStepwise2018]
- Classification and regression trees (also called decision trees) chose from all the variables together and suggest interactions [@oldenMachineLearningMethods2008]; for model selection you propose the models' interactions based on prior knowledge or hypotheses about how the data were formed



#### Implementations and controversies

- `AICcmodavg` R package has a vignette with examples and details [@mazerolleModelSelectionMultimodel2023].  Open software.

- Basic difficulties are covered in @andersonAvoidingPitfallsWhen2002. 

-  @burnhamAICModelSelection2011 provides a basic summary as well as how to use multi-model inference (also called model averaging).

- @harrisonBriefIntroductionMixed2018a covers multi-model inference as well as using mixed models as the base models to compare.  Open access.

- Model averaging has some controversies about how to implement correctly [@cadeModelAveragingMuddled2015].

### Most technical

Burnham, Kenneth P, and David Raymond Anderson. 2008. Model Selection and Multimodel Inference: A Practical Information-Theoretic Approach. New York, NY, USA: Springer.
